content:
These notes follow Stanford CS336, Lecture 5 on GPUs and TPUs. TFLOPS measures trillions of floating-point operations per second.
Part 1. GPU Architecture GPUs have many small compute units and devote less hardware to caching and control than CPUs typically do. GPUs are optimized for throughput, while CPUs are optimized for low latency.
Each streaming multiprocessor (SM) contains many streaming processors (SPs). CUDA cores perform scalar operations. Tensor Cores accelerate matrix multiplication and accumulation.
Threads, Blocks, and Warps Threads run the same kernel in parallel, typically on different inputs. Blocks group threads that share a region of memory and can cooperate. Each block runs on one SM, and an SM can host multiple blocks. Warps are groups of 32 consecutively numbered threads that the GPU schedules together. Each thread can access its own registers and the shared memory of its block. Data shared across blocks generally goes through global memory, which is backed by GPU device memory and is slower to access than on-chip storage.
TPUs feature large matrix multiplication units, fast memory, and lightweight control. GPUs are also massively parallel, and the single-instruction, multiple-thread (SIMT) model makes that parallelism straightforward to program. Threads are lightweight, and adding SMs can scale workloads with enough parallel work.
Compute throughput has grown faster than memory bandwidth, so making good use of the memory hierarchy matters for performance.
Part 2. Understanding GPU Performance The Roofline Model Operational intensity is the number of floating-point operations per byte transferred. Throughput is the number of floating-point operations per second. The sloped region on the left is memory-bound. The flat region on the right is compute-bound.
Dense matrix multiplication processes all entries, including zeros. Sparse matrix multiplication can skip work associated with zero entries.
Control Divergence and Lower Precision Control divergence. When threads in a warp take different branches, they may have to execute the paths separately. For suitable operations, a kernel can use an execution mask to control which lanes participate.
Lower precision. Fewer bits per value means fewer bytes to move. Modern GPUs support low-precision and mixed-precision operations.
FP16 and BF16 can be used for matrix multiplication and pointwise operations. Reductions such as sums, softmax, and normalization often use FP32 accumulation even when inputs are in FP16. Adding small values to a large sum can introduce rounding errors. Dynamic range matters for operations such as powers, exponentials, and loss calculations. FP32 and BF16 offer a wider exponent range than FP16. MXFP8 scaling factors use E8M0, with eight exponent bits and zero mantissa bits.
Operator Fusion and Recomputation Operator fusion combines operations in one kernel so intermediate results can stay near the compute units, reducing trips to global memory.
torch.compile can automatically fuse some straightforward operations. Recomputation discards selected activations in the forward pass and regenerates them during the backward pass to save memory.
Memory Coalescing, Tiling, and Scheduling Memory coalescing combines nearby accesses by threads in a warp into fewer memory transactions. In the example below, the threads’ addresses fall within one burst segment.
Tiling divides matrix multiplication into blocks so threads can reuse data. Tile sizes that do not fit the matrix dimensions and poorly aligned accesses can limit performance.
Aligning dimensions to a multiple of 32 can be faster than aligning to a multiple of 16, depending on the kernel and hardware. Grouping and ordering threads to reuse shared memory can also reduce global memory accesses.
Wave quantization occurs when the number of tiles does not line up with the available SMs, leaving some SMs idle in the last wave.
Part 3. FlashAttention The output projection, shown as P_mix, mixes the outputs of the attention heads. Computing all pairs of attention scores has quadratic complexity in sequence length.
FlashAttention tiles the query, key, and value computations and fuses the operations. Its incremental softmax tracks a running maximum and a running normalization sum. When a new tile changes the maximum, the previous sum and output contributions are rescaled so they remain on the same scale. Subtracting the maximum before exponentiation makes softmax numerically stable.
summary: Notes from CS336 on GPU architecture, the roofline model, and the techniques that come together in FlashAttention.
title: A Glance at GPUs and TPUs Through CS336

Paper: RollPacker: Taming Long-Tail Rollouts for RL Post-Training with Tail Batching
The Long-Tail Distribution Problem The long-tail distribution of response lengths remains a problem.
Tail Batching A rollout stage may fall short of the number of prompts or responses required to form an effective batch. RollPacker addresses this through speculative execution: it overprovisions requests while selectively retaining only the fastest completions. Perhaps this idea is inspired by speculative decoding.
Systematically excluding long prompts distorts the training sample distribution and may harm model performance. My understanding is that preserving the original sample distribution helps avoid this issue.
During stream execution, gradients for completed responses are computed and buffered, but no updates are applied to the model parameters or optimizer state.
Adaptive Parallelism Short rounds impose greater GPU memory pressure because speculative execution launches more concurrent requests, potentially triggering preemption. Increasing the tensor-parallel (TP) size can mitigate this pressure, but it also introduces communication overhead.
RollPacker profiles memory usage offline and selects the optimal TP configuration online.
To limit cross-node communication, TP groups are confined to a single GPU server.
Reward Scheduler The reward scheduler operates asynchronously. Its optimizations include:
Adjusting sandbox timeouts. Dynamically sharing GPUs for judge models. Most layers of the judge LLM are offloaded to host memory, and their parameters are streamed over PCIe in coordination with activation computation on the GPU. Stream Trainer Some GPUs may become idle when their assigned requests finish early. These rollout GPUs can then be repurposed for training.
A heuristic algorithm decides when to reassign GPUs and which GPUs to reassign. This allows training and rollout to overlap.
To preserve training semantics, the stream trainer adjusts the loss scales and defers gradient updates until streaming concludes.
Topics to Learn Next torch.cuda.Stream DAPO Reference RollPacker: Taming Long-Tail Rollouts for RL Post-Training with Tail Batching.
Figures reproduced from the RollPacker paper are credited to the original authors.
summary: Notes on RollPacker’s approach to long-tail rollouts in synchronous RL: tail batching, adaptive parallelism, reward scheduling, and stream-based training.
title: RollPacker: Proposing a Synchronous Algorithm and Addressing Its Challenges

Paper: PrefixFlow: Training-Time KV Caching for Schedule-Level Prefix Reuse in LLM RL Training
Motivation There has been limited work on prefix reuse during training. The related mechanisms in SGLang and vLLM support forward passes only.
The loss may be computed only over the suffix, but gradients still flow to prefix-side parameters through attention. Repeated prefix computation is a real bottleneck.
Workloads with a high prefix ratio include RAG, multimodal tasks, and long-context QA.
During backpropagation, exchanging the order of summation and matrix multiplication yields an equivalent result.
Disadvantages of Using a Single Computation Graph Prefix and suffix computation have heterogeneous context-parallelism requirements, leaving suffix-heavy ranks on the critical path. Prefix activations cannot be offloaded until the graph has finished executing. Pipeline parallelism requires many microbatches, but one graph per group yields only a few. Reducing computation does not always lead to shorter steps or lower memory usage.
Advantages of Schedule-Level Prefix Reuse Context parallelism can be balanced separately for the prefix and suffix. Prefix activations can be offloaded between phases. Pipeline parallelism can benefit from many microbatches. Suffix forward and backward passes can be scheduled more flexibly. Key Design Phase A: Prefix forward. Phase B: Suffix microbatches. Phase C: Prefix backward. Inject the accumulated gK/gV cache into the retained prefix graph and run one shared prefix backward pass. Offloading Mechanism PrefixFlow keeps the hot cache resident, offloads dormant tensors to a pinned host-memory pool, and asynchronously prefetches them for Phase C. It reinvests the released high-bandwidth memory (HBM) in suffix work.
These optimizations all benefit Phase B: they allow larger suffix waves, longer suffixes, and more expensive transient state to remain resident.
Note that one wave can contain multiple microbatches.
Context Parallelism Under context parallelism (CP), each layer must all-gather the prefix K/V for suffix attention and reduce gK/gV back to the owning prefix shards. Prefetching the all-gathered K/V across layers accelerates this process.
This case is more challenging than those addressed by existing approaches such as DeepSpeed Ulysses and Ring Attention.
In Phase B, balancing prefix and suffix work together is difficult. This is also why reusing the prefix within a single computation graph offers limited improvements.
Solution: Balance CP in Separate Stages For non-attention operators, token-wise work is balanced within a single computation mode. For attention, CP algorithms can be applied independently. Gather prefix K/V as read-only data, then reduce the gradients back to the owning prefix shards. Pipeline Parallelism Switch phases locally within each pipeline stage. Suffix forward passes must wait for the required prefix forward computation to finish, rather than for a global phase barrier.
Expert Parallelism Use Rollout Routing Replay, assuming dropless MoE layers.
Implementation Details Framework: TorchTitan.
Phase A does not expose its live graph directly to Phase B. Instead, it creates detached cached leaves for suffix attention and registers coupling hooks on the live prefix keys and values.
Each Phase-B suffix microbatch step builds a short-lived suffix graph, calls backward without retaining the live prefix graph, and accumulates the resulting coupling gradients in the cached leaves.
Phase B is the main target for torch.compile. Phase-A capture and Phase-C delayed backward rely on autograd.
Experiment Design Parallelism Trajectory alignment under composed parallelism. Phase-B prefetching and balancing. Pipeline-parallel stage-local phase switching. Real RL Loop End-to-end performance in terms of training quality (reward and actor loss) and efficiency. Synchronization also improves because waiting times are shorter. No amplification of drift over the replayed trajectory. Speedup varies with the prefix-to-suffix ratio and whether compilation is enabled. Offloading dormant prefix activations creates memory headroom and enables faster suffix execution. Future Directions Kernel-level reuse and schedule-level reuse are complementary. Tree-structured RL data. Long single sequences. Reference PrefixFlow: Training-Time KV Caching for Schedule-Level Prefix Reuse in LLM RL Training.
Figures reproduced from the PrefixFlow paper are credited to the original authors.
summary: Notes on training-time prefix reuse in PrefixFlow: the three-phase schedule, activation offloading, composed parallelism, and experimental design.
title: PrefixFlow: Solid Infra Work

content:
How to design a novel architecture with a novel RL algorithm.
Paper: AReaL: A Large-Scale Asynchronous Reinforcement Learning System for Language Reasoning
Challenges Switching between training and generation. Unequal output lengths. Inconsistent policies and stale data. Synchronous systems reduce the batch size per GPU, leading to memory-I/O-bound execution and poor scalability. System Architecture Interruptible rollout workers belong to the generation stage. The interrupt request is “Update Weights.”
Trainer workers accumulate data until the buffer reaches the batch size.
Rollout controller:
Read data and invoke generation → Send responses to the reward service → Store trajectories and rewards in the buffer → Update the model → Update the workers.
Equipped Algorithm For Staleness η represents the maximum permitted staleness in each training batch. Prioritize older trajectories from the data buffer to form a training batch. The rollout controller tracks both the generated samples N_r and policy version i from the parameter server. Favor a large η. In practice, use the parameters before updating as the proximal policy.
For Better RL Results Compared with PPO:
The outer importance ratio always uses the behavior policy as the denominator. The key choice is the trust-region ratio using the proximal policy. Implementation Details I Should Know CPU work: Rule-based computation and TCP-based data transfer. Separate threads and pipelining: Overlap GPU generation and CPU operations. Asyncio coroutines: Avoid mutually blocking waits in the rollout worker. Batching: A padding-free sequence-packing strategy coupled with a dynamic allocation algorithm. Dynamic Batching Instead of using a fixed batch size for sequences of different lengths, AReaL recombines sequences into batches through a greedy algorithm. Long sequences can cause OOM, while inefficient batching can underutilize memory.
Sequence Packing This is not this paper’s innovation. Concatenation enables padding-free execution with attention isolation.
Evaluation Designs Comprehensive comparisons against state-of-the-art open-source frameworks across model sizes. Strong-scaling analysis with varying compute resources. Ablation studies validating design choices. Baseline: veRL.
Ablation: Decoupled PPO.
Insight Allocating 75% of resources to inference and 25% to training demonstrated higher training throughput.
My Prospect of the Future MoE architecture optimization. More design work around the differences between training and generation. Preliminaries Generation involves autoregressive decoding, which requires efficient KV-cache management and optimized decoding kernels.
Training requires careful orchestration of data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism strategies.
Reference AReaL: A Large-Scale Asynchronous Reinforcement Learning System for Language Reasoning.
The AReaL paper figures reproduced in these notes are credited to the original authors. The PPO-Clip illustration is retained from the original notes.
summary: A second look at RL infrastructure through AReaL: asynchronous generation and training, interruptible rollouts, policy staleness, and implementation details.
title: The Second Glance with Infra: AReaL

content:
Through this paper, I understand the research pipeline in infra, especially in how to design an infrastructure for a specific popular training algorithm, which serves as a solid base for me to explore more in this area. By the way, I know a few professional explanations and code organization in this process.
Paper: HybridFlow: A Flexible and Efficient RLHF Framework
Basic Knowledge DP: Data Parallelism, more model replicas. TP: Tensor Parallelism, divide matrix into little matrices. PP: Pipeline Parallelism, attention for one GPU and MLP for another. Inference: One forward pass. Generation: Multiple forward passes. All-Gather: Collect data from all GPUs and each one then gets a complete copy of data. Reduce-Scatter: Collect and reduce data from all GPUs and then scatter part of reduced data to each GPU. Rank: Distributed process ID. Existing Works’ Shortcomings Single controller avoids complex point-to-point send and receive workflows, boosting more flexibility.
Analysis of RLHF (Take PPO as an Example) Actor training: Computation bound, more TP, more PP, less DP. Generation: GPU memory bound, more DP, less TP, less PP due to no gradient, no backward, no optimizer. Model resharding leads to memory redundancy. Code Realization APIs encapsulate distributed computation and support 3D parallelism, ZeRO, and PyTorch FSDP.
Python decorator: Additional functions without changing the code.
NCCL communication primitives collect and concatenate model parameters in each micro-DP group during the transition between training and generation.
Related Work Analysis DeepSpeed-Colocation: Actor training and generation in the same GPU, model resharding between training and generation. OpenRLHF: Each model placed on separate devices, two copies of generation and training models. NeMo-Aligner: Actor/Ref colocate, Critic-Reward colocate, same model for generation and training. Single controller: Insufficient for large GPU distribution. Multi-controller: Inflexible to implement various RLHF workflows. Key Design Single-controller in inter-node. Multi-controller in intra-node. Hierarchical API Use resource pools to manage GPUs. Configure models with different parallelism and then allocate devices. Asynchronous execution using data futures. 3D-Hybrid Engine Workflow: Switch Between Actor Training and Generation Dg is determined by p, t, pg, dg.
All-gather weights → Load prompts → Generate and all-gather responses → Partition weights → Model update → All-gather weights.
Zero Memory Redundancy All-gather within micro-DP groups enables both efficiency and no redundancy.
Auto Mapping Auto parallel + simulation + double nested loop for best mapping.
Nested loop:
Find best placements for actor, critic, reference, reward. Find best allocation for each group. Experiment Design Compare throughput across three RLHF algorithms. Compare throughput under different model placements, GPU counts, and model sizes. Compare the time of different transitions across GPU counts and model sizes. Break down actor model execution time under different parallelism strategies and model sizes. Design Principles Flexible. Efficient. Simple for users. Avoid a central bottleneck. Reference Guangming Sheng et al. HybridFlow: A Flexible and Efficient RLHF Framework, 2024.
The paper figures reproduced in these notes are from HybridFlow; credit belongs to the original authors.
summary: My first exploration of RLHF infrastructure through HybridFlow: controller paradigms, hierarchical APIs, the 3D-HybridEngine, and automatic device mapping.
title: First Meet Infra: HybridFlow
